metadata.file_name: 122. Schmitz & Sonnleitner (2025). Evaluating AI‑generated vs. human‑written reading comprehension passages: an expert SWOT analysis and comparative study for an educational large‑scale assessment.pdf
metadata.title: Evaluating AI-generated vs. human-written reading comprehension passages: an expert SWOT analysis and comparative study for an educational large-scale assessment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used an online blinded review questionnaire (LimeSurvey) with a snowball-recruited sample of N=89 reviewers who evaluated a small set of six reading comprehension texts (four GPT-4 generated and two human-written). The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme; participants were not drawn via a probability sample of students or schools from ÉpStan. Because the analysis is based on human ratings and group comparisons (e.g., MANOVA/Tukey HSD) rather than ILSA achievement PV estimation, there is no PV-based weighting requirement. Consequently, no weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is specified, and the results should be interpreted as evidence about perceived text quality rather than population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not analyze ILSA-style cognitive achievement outcomes with Plausible Values; instead, it uses Likert-scale human judgments of text quality dimensions and a subjective discernibility judgment (human vs AI). Missing-data handling is not described for the questionnaire items; the only explicit attrition information is that 72 of 161 enrolled participants did not complete the survey, leaving N=89. This means the paper provides limited transparency on how partially missing item responses (if any) were treated within the completed cases.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited via snowball sampling and completed a three-week online blinded review. The analytic sample comprised only those who completed the questionnaire (N=89) after excluding non-completers (72 of 161). Reviewers evaluated six German reading comprehension texts (two human-written and four GPT-4 generated) presented in randomized order; the manuscript does not report additional exclusions based on demographics or language proficiency beyond the general assumption that the sample could evaluate German texts in the Luxembourgish primary context.

main_findings.dataset_used: ÉpStan-aligned German Grade 5 reading comprehension texts (GPT-4 generation; human vs AI; narrative & informative genres)
main_findings.target_variable: Text quality ratings (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, adequacy)
main_findings.performance_metrics: MANOVA (Pillai’s Trace) for narrative: V=0.169, F(10, 522)=4.82, p<0.001; MANOVA for informative: V=0.077, F(10, 522)=2.093, p=0.023. Narrative post-hoc: significant differences in readability, engagement, coherence, adequacy; correctness showed no significant differences. Informative post-hoc: significant differences in readability (human vs one-shot), AI one-shot vs zero-shot (readability, coherence, adequacy). Descriptives: all mean dimension scores >4 on 5-point Likert; Cronbach’s alpha per dimension ~0.71–0.89; ceiling effects reported.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ÉpStan-aligned German Grade 5 reading comprehension texts the study compared human-written versus GPT-4 texts under zero-shot and one-shot prompting and evaluated five human-rated quality dimensions, finding that overall text quality was similarly high and that prompt type mattered by genre (one-shot better for informative texts; human-written better for narratives). This indicates that generative AI can support reading-text development in large-scale assessment contexts, but prompt strategy and genre-specific oversight are necessary to preserve engagement and coherence.

main_findings.dataset_used: ÉpStan-aligned German Grade 5 reading comprehension texts (blinded authorship discernibility; narrative & informative genres)
main_findings.target_variable: Authorship discernibility (human vs AI; correct identification rates)
main_findings.performance_metrics: No text type achieved >50% correct identification. Narrative: mean accuracy 45.67% (human-written higher correct identification: 48.32% for narrative human-written; AI discernibility lower for narrative one-shot and zero-shot). Informative: mean accuracy 41.20% (informative zero-shot highest correct identification 49.44%; informative one-shot correct identification 31.46%). Substantial undecided responses (~1/6 to 1/4) and misclassification rates reported; discernibility differed by genre and prompting.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ÉpStan-aligned German Grade 5 reading comprehension texts the study assessed whether reviewers could distinguish human-written from GPT-4-generated passages and found that reviewers could not reliably identify authorship, with no condition exceeding 50% correct and many undecided responses. This indicates that GPT-4 can emulate human-like reading passages sufficiently to challenge authorship detection, so assessment programs should rely on human-in-the-loop validation and provenance controls rather than on reviewer discernibility alone.

data.outcome_summary: This mixed-methods study evaluated GPT-4’s usefulness for generating German reading comprehension passages aligned with Luxembourg’s ÉpStan context, focusing on Grade 5 narrative and informative genres. In a qualitative focus group (N=6 SMEs), experts developed a Text Analysis Cognitive Model (TACM) and SWOT-informed constraints for text generation. In a quantitative blinded review, N=89 participants rated six texts on five Likert-scale quality dimensions (readability, correctness, coherence, engagement, adequacy) and judged whether each text appeared human-written or AI-generated. Results showed ceiling-level quality (all means >4) and genre-dependent prompt effects: one-shot prompting performed best for informative texts, while human-written texts were superior for narratives in engagement/coherence/adequacy; correctness did not differ significantly across narrative conditions. Authorship discernibility was weak (no condition >50% correct; many undecided), implying that AI-generated texts can be human-like, but human oversight and governance are required. Limitations include small stimulus set (four AI texts) and lack of reported missing-item handling for the questionnaire.
